nodes.label: Abdülhamid deposed; Mehmed V
nodes.full: Abdülhamid II restored the constitution on 24 July 1908 under the pressure of the revolution in Macedonia, and after the failed counter-revolt of April 1909 parliament voted his deposition on 27 April; his brother Mehmed V Reşad (1909–1918), then 64, was a constitutional figurehead and left government to the cabinets and the Committee of Union and Progress. He proclaimed the jihad in November 1914 and died in July 1918.
nodes.src: Şükrü Hanioğlu, Preparation for a Revolution (2001); Feroz Ahmad, The Young Turks (1969); Erik Zürcher, Turkey: A Modern History (1993).

nodes.label: Enver, Talat and Cemal
nodes.full: After the coup of 23 January 1913, when Enver Bey and his friends burst into the Sublime Porte during a cabinet meeting and shot the minister of war, the Committee of Union and Progress ruled the empire through three men: Enver Pasha, minister of war from 1914, Talat Pasha, minister of the interior and from 1917 grand vizier, and Cemal Pasha, minister of the navy and commander in Syria. At the armistice in 1918 all three fled abroad, and were sentenced to death in absentia by an Ottoman court in 1919.
nodes.src: Ahmad 1969; Hanioğlu, A Brief History of the Late Ottoman Empire (2008); Zürcher 1993; Taner Akçam, A Shameful Act (2006).

nodes.label: Mehmed VI
nodes.full: Mehmed VI, the last sultan, who came to the throne in July 1918 at 57, appointed cabinets that were ready to deal with the Allied occupation and the nationalist movement, signed the Treaty of Sèvres through his delegates in 1920 and declared the nationalists rebels; after the Grand National Assembly abolished the sultanate on 1 November 1922 he left Istanbul on a British warship on 17 November, and died in San Remo in 1926.
nodes.src: Zürcher 1993; Hanioğlu 2008; Hasan Kayalı, Arabs and Young Turks (1997).

nodes.label: Grand viziers
nodes.full: The grand viziers of the period included Hüseyin Hilmi Pasha, Kâmil Pasha (1908–1909, 1912–1913), Mahmud Şevket Pasha (1913, killed in June 1913), Prince Said Halim Pasha (1913–1917), Talat Pasha (1917–1918), Ahmed İzzet Pasha, and Damad Ferid Pasha (1919–1920), the Liberal Entente leader who signed Sèvres; during the CUP years the real power lay in the Central Committee and the war ministry.
nodes.src: Ahmad 1969; Zürcher 1993; Zürcher, The Unionist Factor (1984).

nodes.label: Mustafa Kemal and the Assembly
nodes.full: Mustafa Kemal, a general who had been at Gallipoli and had gone to Samsun in May 1919 as inspector, resigned his commission and, as head of the Representative Committee of the Erzurum and Sivas congresses, led the national movement; the Grand National Assembly opened in Ankara on 23 April 1920 with him as president, and he was commander in chief after the victory at Sakarya (1921) with the title Gazi, and directed the final offensive of August 1922.
nodes.src: Zürcher 1993; Andrew Mango, Atatürk (1999); Nutuk (1927).

nodes.label: Sharif Hussein
nodes.full: Hussein ibn Ali, appointed Sharif and Emir of Mecca by Abdülhamid II in 1908, began in 1915 the correspondence with the British High Commissioner McMahon, proclaimed the Arab revolt on 10 June 1916 and took the title King of the Hejaz and of the Arabs in October; he was the Hashemite ruler of the Hejaz until his abdication in 1924 after Saudi pressure, and father of Faisal and Abdullah.
nodes.src: Joshua Teitelbaum, The Rise and Fall of the Hashimite Kingdom of Arabia (2001); Eugene Rogan, The Fall of the Ottomans (2015).

nodes.label: Revolution and counter-revolt
nodes.full: The mutiny of officers of the Third Army in Macedonia in July 1908, led by Niyazi Bey and Enver, forced the sultan to restore the constitution, and in April 1909 troops of the Istanbul garrison, with the support of religious students and the Liberal Union, rose against the CUP in the counter-revolt of 31 Mart; Mahmud Şevket's Action Army marched from Salonica, retook the city on 24 April and had the sultan deposed. Large massacres of Armenians in Adana in April 1909 killed some 20,000 or more.
nodes.src: Hanioğlu 2001; Ahmad 1969; Zürcher 1993; Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: Italo-Turkish war
nodes.full: Italy declared war on 29 September 1911 and landed at Tripoli and Benghazi; the Ottoman officers, among them Enver and Mustafa Kemal, organised the Sanusi and local resistance in Cyrenaica, and Italian forces seized Rhodes and the Dodecanese; the Treaty of Ouchy in October 1912, signed under the pressure of the Balkan crisis, gave Libya to Italy, with a nominal recognition of the sultan's religious authority.
nodes.src: Treaty of Ouchy (1912); Zürcher 1993; Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Balkan Wars
nodes.full: Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro attacked in October 1912 and in a few weeks took almost all the European provinces, with Salonica falling to Greece in November and Edirne to Bulgaria in March 1913; Enver retook Edirne in the second Balkan War in July. The empire lost about 83 per cent of its European territory and some 69 per cent of its European population, and Albania became independent in November 1912; hundreds of thousands of Muslims fled.
nodes.src: Treaty of London (1913), Treaty of Bucharest (1913), Treaty of Constantinople (1913); Richard Hall, The Balkan Wars (2000); Zürcher 1993.

nodes.label: Raid on the Sublime Porte
nodes.full: When the government of Kâmil Pasha seemed ready to cede Edirne to Bulgaria, Enver and a band of officers burst into the Sublime Porte, shot the minister of war Nazım Pasha and forced the grand vizier to resign; Mahmud Şevket Pasha, who became grand vizier, was assassinated in June, which led to a repression of the opposition and a more openly authoritarian CUP regime.
nodes.src: Ahmad 1969; Zürcher 1993; Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: Entry into the war
nodes.full: A secret alliance with Germany was signed on 2 August 1914, and when the German cruisers Goeben and Breslau reached the Dardanelles on 10 August the empire took them over; on 29 October the Ottoman fleet under German command bombarded Odessa and other Russian ports, and Russia, Britain and France declared war in early November. Enver and Talat made the decision with the war minister's circle; a part of the cabinet resigned.
nodes.src: Rogan 2015; Mustafa Aksakal, The Ottoman Road to War in 1914 (2008).

nodes.label: Sarıkamış
nodes.full: Enver Pasha, taking the command of the Third Army himself, launched an encircling winter offensive against the Russians at Sarıkamış in the mountains of the Caucasus front in December 1914, and in deep snow and cold, with poor supply, the army lost, by most counts, the greater part of some 90,000 men to frost, typhus and Russian counter-attack; the defeat left eastern Anatolia open to Russia.
nodes.src: Edward Erickson, Ordered to Die (2001); Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Suez and Sinai
nodes.full: Cemal Pasha's force crossed the Sinai and attacked the Suez Canal on 3 February 1915 and was repulsed; a second attempt in August 1916 was defeated at Romani by British and Anzac forces. The empire's aim of seizing Egypt failed, and the British began the advance across the Sinai that led to the capture of Jerusalem.
nodes.src: Erickson 2001; Rogan 2015; Cemal Pasha, Memories of a Turkish Statesman (1922).

nodes.label: Gallipoli
nodes.full: After the Allied fleet lost three battleships on the minefield on 18 March 1915, British, French and Anzac troops landed on the peninsula on 25 April; Ottoman divisions under Mustafa Kemal, Esat Pasha and the German commander Liman von Sanders held the heights through months of trench warfare and the Allies withdrew in December 1915–January 1916, with some 250,000 casualties on each side. It was the empire's greatest victory in the war.
nodes.src: Erickson 2001; Robin Prior, Gallipoli: The End of the Myth (2009); Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Kut and Mesopotamia
nodes.full: An Anglo-Indian force that had reached within 40 kilometres of Baghdad was defeated at Ctesiphon in November 1915 and besieged by Halil Pasha's Sixth Army at Kut al-Amara, where General Townshend surrendered on 29 April 1916 with some 13,000 men, of whom many died as prisoners; the British renewed the advance and took Baghdad on 11 March 1917 and Mosul after the armistice.
nodes.src: Erickson 2001; Rogan 2015; Charles Townshend, When God Made Hell (2010).

nodes.label: Armenian genocide
nodes.full: From April 1915 the government arrested the Armenian elite of Istanbul, and from May deported the Armenians of the eastern provinces and later of most of Anatolia to the Syrian desert; men were separated and killed, and the columns of women, children and old people died of massacre, starvation and disease or were absorbed into Muslim households. The estimates of those who died are from 600,000 to 1.5 million, with most scholars at about a million; the great majority of genocide scholars and many states call it genocide, while the Turkish state rejects that term and speaks of wartime relocations and the deaths of Armenians and Muslims alike.
nodes.src: Raymond Kévorkian, The Armenian Genocide (2011); Taner Akçam, A Shameful Act (2006); Ronald Suny, They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else (2015); Hilmar Kaiser.

nodes.label: Sayfo
nodes.full: Assyrians, Chaldeans and Syriacs in Hakkari, Tur Abdin, Siirt and Urmia were massacred and deported in 1915–1918 by Ottoman troops, Kurdish tribes and irregulars, with estimates of 150,000 to 300,000 dead, perhaps half of the community; the Assyrians call the events Sayfo, the Sword, and a growing number of scholars and parliaments treat them as part of the same genocidal policy.
nodes.src: David Gaunt, Massacres, Resistance, Protectors (2006); Hannibal Travis, Genocide in the Middle East (2010).

nodes.label: Arab Revolt
nodes.full: Sharif Hussein's sons Faisal and Abdullah opened the Arab revolt by attacking the Ottoman garrisons in the Hejaz on 10 June 1916; Medina held out under Fahreddin Pasha until after the armistice, and Faisal's bedouin and regular troops, with British subsidies, gold, advisers such as T. E. Lawrence and Egyptian officers, took Aqaba in July 1917 and entered Damascus in October 1918. The revolt was a sideshow in military terms and the most powerful symbol of Arab nationalism.
nodes.src: Rogan 2015; Teitelbaum 2001; T. E. Lawrence, Seven Pillars of Wisdom (1926); Eliezer Tauber, The Arab Movements in World War I (1993).

nodes.label: Palestine and Megiddo
nodes.full: General Allenby's Egyptian Expeditionary Force took Beersheba on 31 October 1917 and Jerusalem on 9 December, and in the battle of Megiddo of 19–25 September 1918 broke the Ottoman Seventh and Eighth armies, led by Liman von Sanders, and reached Damascus and Aleppo before the armistice; the Ottoman army in Syria was destroyed.
nodes.src: Erickson 2001; Rogan 2015; Matthew Hughes, Allenby and British Strategy in the Middle East (1999).

nodes.label: Mudros and occupation
nodes.full: The armistice signed on the British warship Agamemnon at Mudros on 30 October 1918 demobilised the army, opened the Straits, gave the Allies the right to occupy strategic points and put the Ottoman state at their mercy; British, French and Italian forces entered Istanbul on 13 November 1918 and, after the nationalist movement started, formally occupied the city on 16 March 1920.
nodes.src: Armistice of Mudros (1918); Zürcher 1993; Mango 1999.

nodes.label: National struggle
nodes.full: The Greek landing at Smyrna on 15 May 1919 and the advance into Anatolia led to a war with the nationalist army, in which the Turks held the Greeks at the Sakarya in August–September 1921 and in the Great Offensive of 26 August 1922 destroyed their army at Dumlupınar; Izmir was retaken on 9 September and burned a few days after. The war ended with the armistice of Mudanya on 11 October 1922.
nodes.src: Zürcher 1993; Mango 1999; Michael Llewellyn Smith, Ionian Vision (1973).

nodes.label: Restored constitution
nodes.full: The constitution of 1876 was restored on 24 July 1908, elections were held in autumn and the parliament, with Turks, Arabs, Greeks, Armenians, Albanians and others, met in December; amendments of August 1909 made the sultan's powers subject to the ministers and the chamber, restricted the right of association and dismissal, and strengthened the cabinet, the Ottoman version of a constitutional monarchy.
nodes.src: Constitution (1876, as amended 1909); Ahmad 1969; Zürcher 1993.

nodes.label: Secret agreements
nodes.full: During the war the Allies concluded the Constantinople Agreement of March–April 1915, promising Russia the city and the Straits, the Hussein–McMahon exchange of 1915–1916 on an Arab state, the Sykes–Picot Agreement of May 1916 between Britain and France, dividing the Arab provinces into zones of direct control and influence, and the Treaty of St-Jean-de-Maurienne of 1917 for Italy; the Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917 added a promise of a Jewish national home in Palestine.
nodes.src: Sykes–Picot Agreement (1916); Hussein–McMahon correspondence (1915–1916); Balfour Declaration (1917); Rogan 2015; Eugene Rogan and Avi Shlaim (eds.), The War for Palestine (2001).

nodes.label: Deportation and property laws
nodes.full: A provisional law of 27 May 1915, the Temporary Law of Deportation, authorised military commanders to deport populations suspected of espionage or treason, and a law of 10 June and the Abandoned Property Law of 26 September 1915 regulated the liquidation of the property of those deported, which was registered by commissions and in many cases sold or taken by officials and neighbours; these measures formed the legal framework of the deportation of the Armenians.
nodes.src: Provisional Law of 27 May 1915; Law of 26 September 1915; Akçam 2006; Uğur Ümit Üngör and Mehmet Polatel, Confiscation and Destruction (2011).

nodes.label: Capitulations abolished
nodes.full: Using the outbreak of the European war, the Ottoman government declared on 9 September 1914 the unilateral abolition of the capitulations from 1 October, which had been the main limit on the sovereignty of the state for centuries; the powers protested but could not reverse it, and the end of the regime was confirmed at Lausanne in 1923.
nodes.src: Note of 9 September 1914; Maurits van den Boogert, The Capitulations and the Ottoman Legal System (2005); Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Treaty of Sèvres
nodes.full: The treaty imposed on the Ottoman government left the sultan with Constantinople and a rump in Anatolia, put the Straits under an international commission, gave Izmir and its hinterland to Greece for five years, provided for an Armenian state, an autonomous Kurdistan, and French and Italian zones, and kept the capitulations; signed by Damad Ferid's delegates but never ratified, it was destroyed by the nationalists' victories.
nodes.src: Treaty of Sèvres (1920); Zürcher 1993; Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Sultanate abolished
nodes.full: After the Allies invited both the government at Istanbul and the Ankara government to the peace conference at Lausanne, the Grand National Assembly voted on 1 November 1922 to separate and abolish the sultanate, leaving the caliphate to an Ottoman prince, and Mehmed VI left on 17 November; the Ottoman dynasty had ruled for 623 years according to the customary count.
nodes.src: Law of 1 November 1922; Zürcher 1993; Mango 1999.

nodes.label: Jihad of 1914
nodes.full: After the declaration of war the Şeyhülislam issued five fatwas and the sultan-caliph proclaimed a holy war on 14 November 1914 against Britain, France and Russia, in the hope of stirring Muslims in the Allies' empires; the call, printed in many languages and promoted by Germany, had little effect among Muslim subjects of the powers, and Sharif Hussein's revolt contradicted it.
nodes.src: Fatwas and proclamation (14 November 1914); Rogan 2015; Aksakal 2008.

nodes.label: Conversions and churches
nodes.full: Many Armenian women and children saved themselves or were taken by conversion to Islam and absorption into Muslim households, a part of the deportation policy of assimilation; churches, monasteries and schools were seized, destroyed or turned to other uses, and the Armenian patriarchate and the property of the church were taken over by the state commissions.
nodes.src: Kévorkian 2011; Akçam 2012; Ara Sarafian (ed.), United States Official Records on the Armenian Genocide (2004).

nodes.label: The last caliph
nodes.full: The Grand National Assembly elected on 18 November 1922 the sultan's cousin Abdülmecid II as caliph, with spiritual powers only and without any temporal power; he held the office until 3 March 1924, when the Assembly abolished the caliphate and sent the dynasty into exile, ending the caliphate that had been associated with the Ottoman house for four centuries.
nodes.src: Law of 1 November 1922; Law of 3 March 1924; Zürcher 1993.

nodes.label: First Ottoman film
nodes.full: Fuat Uzkınay, an officer, filmed on 14 November 1914 the demolition of the Russian memorial at San Stefano (Ayastefanos), a film now lost but seen as the first Ottoman documentary; under the Central Army Cinema Directorate of 1915 other newsreels and documentaries were shot, and Muhsin Ertuğrul began the Ottoman film industry after the war.
nodes.src: Nijat Özön, Türk Sineması Tarihi (1962); Gönül Dönmez-Colin, Turkish Cinema (2008).

nodes.label: Independence March
nodes.full: Mehmet Akif Ersoy, a poet and deputy who had written Safahat, wrote the ten stanzas of the İstiklal Marşı (Independence March) in 1921 for the competition of the national government; it was adopted by the Grand National Assembly on 12 March 1921 and became the anthem of the Republic, with Akif's words on faith and the fatherland.
nodes.src: Mehmet Akif Ersoy, Safahat (1911–1933); Zürcher 1993.

nodes.label: Halide Edib
nodes.full: Halide Edib (Adıvar), a teacher and later lecturer at the university, wrote Seviye Talib (1910), Yeni Turan (1912), a novel of a Turkist utopia, and Ateşten Gömlek (1922) on the national struggle, in which she served as a corporal and sergeant; her work shaped women's literature and the idea of the nation.
nodes.src: Halide Edib, The Memoirs of Halidé Edib (1926) and The Turkish Ordeal (1928); Hanioğlu 2008.

nodes.label: Arrest of Armenian writers
nodes.full: On 24 April 1915 and the days that followed the police arrested some 250 Armenian community leaders, writers and deputies; among those killed later were the poets Daniel Varoujan and Siamanto, the novelist Krikor Zohrab and the dramatist Rupen Sevag; the musician Komitas, who was among the deportees, survived physically but never recovered from the shock and lived in a psychiatric hospital until his death in 1935.
nodes.src: Kévorkian 2011; Peter Balakian, The Burning Tigris (2003); Rita Soulahian Kuyumjian, Archeology of Madness (2001).

nodes.label: Gökalp and Turkism
nodes.full: The Turkish Hearths (Türk Ocakları) were founded in 1912 and the journal Türk Yurdu in 1911; Ziya Gökalp, a sociologist from Diyarbakır, in 1913 defined the programme of Turkification, Islamisation and Modernisation and distinguished the culture of the Turkish nation from the civilisation of Islam and of Europe, while the CUP's policies increasingly promoted the Turkish element in the economy and the state.
nodes.src: Ziya Gökalp, The Principles of Turkism (1923; trans. Robert Devereux, 1968); Uriel Heyd, Foundations of Turkish Nationalism (1950); David Kushner, The Rise of Turkish Nationalism (1977).

nodes.label: Arab societies and Congress
nodes.full: Arab societies such as al-Fatat (1911), al-Ahd (1913), the Ottoman Decentralisation Party in Cairo and reform committees in Beirut and Basra demanded Arab rights and administrative decentralisation within the empire, and the Arab Congress of Paris in June 1913 asked for Arab autonomy and the use of Arabic in the Arab provinces; the government's response was a mixture of concession and repression, and the executions in Beirut and Damascus in 1915–1916 of dozens of Arab notables sharpened the break.
nodes.src: Kayalı 1997; George Antonius, The Arab Awakening (1938); Rashid Khalidi, Palestinian Identity (1997).

nodes.label: End of Ottomanism and Wilson
nodes.full: After the armistice some Ottoman intellectuals, among them members of the Wilsonian Principles League of 1919 and the Friends of England, believed that an American mandate over Anatolia would save the empire from partition and the principle of national self-determination would protect its Turkish core; the proposal of a mandate was debated in the Sivas congress of 1919 and rejected in favour of the National Pact of January 1920.
nodes.src: Zürcher 1993; Mango 1999; Hanioğlu 2008; National Pact (28 January 1920).

nodes.label: National economy
nodes.full: The CUP government used the war and the abolition of the capitulations to promote a Muslim Turkish middle class, favouring Turkish traders and companies, taking over the property of deported Armenians and Greeks, and setting up companies such as the Ottoman National Bank (1917); the war profiteers (harp zenginleri) of the period became a visible class.
nodes.src: Zafer Toprak, Türkiye'de Milli İktisat (1982); Çağlar Keyder, State and Class in Turkey (1987); Zürcher 1993.

nodes.label: War debt and inflation
nodes.full: The war was financed by German loans in gold and paper of well over a hundred million pounds, the printing of paper money and requisitions, and prices in Istanbul rose more than twentyfold between 1914 and 1918; wages did not keep up, grain was taken for the army and the cities lacked bread, and the lack of rolling stock and fuel disrupted transport.
nodes.src: Şevket Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire (2000); Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Famine of Syria
nodes.full: The Allied blockade of the coast, a plague of locusts in 1915, requisitions by the army and the profiteering of merchants led to a famine in which some 100,000 to 200,000 people, perhaps a third of the population of Mount Lebanon, died, and many more in the cities of Syria; the question of responsibility, between the Ottoman government of Cemal Pasha and the Allied blockade, is argued.
nodes.src: Linda Schatkowski Schilcher, ‘The Famine of 1915–1918 in Greater Syria’, in Problems of the Modern Middle East in Historical Perspective (1992); Melanie Tanielian, The Charity of War (2018).

nodes.label: Taurus tunnels
nodes.full: The Baghdad Railway was completed through the Taurus and Amanus mountains with the use of forced labour, among them Armenian deportees and prisoners of war, and the line, opened for through traffic in 1918, was a strategic communication line to the Syrian and Mesopotamian fronts; its sections in Syria and Mesopotamia remained incomplete until 1940.
nodes.src: Erickson 2001; Murat Özyüksel, The Berlin–Baghdad Railway (2014); Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Air arm and minefield
nodes.full: Ottoman officers were trained in France and Germany from 1911 for an aviation arm, and the army's air units, with German crews, fought on the Sinai and at Gallipoli; the minelayer Nusret, commanded by Nazmi Bey, laid a line of mines on the night of 7–8 March 1915 that sank three Allied battleships on 18 March, and the Straits' defences were rebuilt with German help.
nodes.src: Erickson 2001; Robin Prior 2009; Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: German alliance
nodes.full: The secret treaty of alliance, signed by the grand vizier Said Halim and the German ambassador Wangenheim, bound the Ottomans to Germany in case Russia attacked, and when the war began the Ottoman cabinet declared neutrality while the war party under Enver prepared the German entry; the German Military Mission under Liman von Sanders had directed the army since December 1913.
nodes.src: Treaty of 2 August 1914; Aksakal 2008; Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Hussein–McMahon
nodes.full: In ten letters between July 1915 and March 1916 the British High Commissioner in Egypt, Sir Henry McMahon, and Sharif Hussein discussed British recognition of an independent Arab state in the Ottoman Arab provinces in return for an Arab revolt; the exclusion of areas west of Damascus, Homs, Hama and Aleppo is the main point of dispute over the extent of the promise, particularly concerning Palestine.
nodes.src: Hussein–McMahon correspondence (1915–1916); Elie Kedourie, In the Anglo-Arab Labyrinth (1976); Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Paris conference
nodes.full: At the conference of 1919 the delegations of Faisal, the Armenian Republic and the Armenian National Delegation under Boghos Nubar, Greece under Venizelos and Zionist leaders made their claims; the Allies sent the King–Crane commission to Syria and Palestine, whose report favouring an American mandate was not adopted, and the question of the Ottoman territories was settled by the mandates of San Remo in April 1920 and the Treaty of Sèvres.
nodes.src: Margaret MacMillan, Paris 1919 (2001); King–Crane Commission report (1919); Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Moscow and Ankara treaties
nodes.full: The Ankara government concluded the Treaty of Moscow with Soviet Russia on 16 March 1921, fixing the eastern border and bringing Soviet gold and arms, and the Treaty of Ankara with France on 20 October 1921, ending the war in Cilicia and Syria and recognising the national government; Italy and Britain then also moved towards contact, and the diplomatic isolation of the Istanbul government deepened.
nodes.src: Treaty of Moscow (1921); Treaty of Ankara (1921); Zürcher 1993; Mango 1999.

nodes.label: Refugees
nodes.full: The Balkan Wars sent some 400,000 Muslims from Macedonia, Thrace and Bulgaria to Anatolia, the wars and deportations of 1914–1918 and 1919–1922 uprooted millions more, among them the Armenians, Greeks and Muslims of the east and the west, and by 1923 the population of Anatolia had changed so that the proportion of non-Muslims was about 2 per cent compared with about 20 per cent before the war.
nodes.src: Kemal Karpat, Ottoman Population 1830–1914 (1985); Justin McCarthy, Death and Exile (1995); Zürcher 1993.

nodes.label: Epidemics and war dead
nodes.full: Typhus, typhoid, cholera, malaria and the influenza of 1918 killed a large share of the soldiers and civilians; the Ottoman military deaths of about 770,000, some 240,000 in battle and nearly 470,000 of disease, and the civilian losses, including Armenians, Muslims and others, make the war's total death toll between two and three million, or about one in seven of the population.
nodes.src: Erickson 2001; Hikmet Özdemir, The Ottoman Army 1914–1918 (2008); Rogan 2015.

nodes.label: Locusts
nodes.full: In the spring of 1915 swarms of locusts struck Syria, Palestine and Lebanon and ate the crops, the first of several poor harvests, and with the requisition of draught animals, the army's demands for grain and the blockade, they were an immediate cause of the famine of the following years.
nodes.src: Schilcher 1992; Tanielian 2018; Cemal Pasha, Memories.

nodes.label: Women in the war
nodes.full: The Ottoman women's movement grew in the press and in associations such as the Society for the Elevation of Women, women entered the university lecture halls in 1914 and the offices and the factories in the war, and the family law of 1917 gave them rights in marriage and divorce; in the national struggle women in Anatolia carried supplies to the front and some, like Halide Edib and Kara Fatma, fought.
nodes.src: Serpil Çakır, Osmanlı Kadın Hareketi (1994); Elizabeth Frierson; Zürcher 1993.

nodes.label: Survivors and orphans
nodes.full: Armenian survivors of the deportations reached Aleppo, Deir ez-Zor, Beirut and Damascus, where relief workers of the American Near East Relief, missionaries and the diplomatic corps, among them Jakob Künzler and Armin Wegner, recorded the camps; after the war tens of thousands of orphans were gathered in orphanages in Syria, Lebanon, Greece and Istanbul, and several thousand women and children were recovered from Muslim households.
nodes.src: Near East Relief reports (1919–1930); Vahram Shemmassian; Keith David Watenpaugh, Bread from Stones (2015).

nodes.label: Soldiers’ letters
nodes.full: Some three million men served in the Ottoman army, most of them Anatolian Muslim peasants, called Mehmetçik, who endured heavy losses from disease, hunger and desertion, which in 1917 reached half a million; the surviving letters, diaries and songs (türkü) such as Çanakkale İçinde record the experience of the front, and the memory of it became part of the founding story of the Republic.
nodes.src: Erickson 2001; Özdemir 2008; Yücel Yanıkdağ, Healing the Nation (2013).

nodes.label: The Greeks of the coast
nodes.full: Ottoman Greeks of the Aegean coast and the Black Sea were expelled in 1914 and put into labour battalions in 1915–1918, with deaths in the tens of thousands, and after 1919 the war with Greece brought massacres and expulsions on both sides, among them the burning of Izmir's Greek and Armenian quarters in September 1922; Greece and Turkey call the Pontic events genocide and a national tragedy respectively, and the exchange of populations of 1923 completed the movement.
nodes.src: Tessa Hofmann (ed.), Verfolgung, Vertreibung und Vernichtung der Christen im Osmanischen Reich (2004); Zürcher 1993; Giles Milton, Paradise Lost (2008).

nodes.label: The Hamidian regime and the Young Turk opposition
nodes.full: Abdülhamid II’s thirty-year personal rule, its schools, officers and informers, and the exile opposition of the Committee of Union and Progress prepared the revolution of 1908.
nodes.src: background — see the Ottoman Empire 1839–1908 folio (ottoman-empire-1839-1908)
